newsitem.title: FRANCE: Talks set to start in French truckers' dispute.
newsitem.headline: Talks set to start in French truckers' dispute.

text.p: Haulage bosses said on Wednesday they had agreed to open talks with striking truck drivers who have blocked roads across France for three days.

Jean Demarne, president of the Union of Transport Federations told reporters that "after the meetings we have had with government authorities, our members have declared themselves in favour of opening talks immediately with the trades unions."
Demarne spoke after a two hour meeting with Transport Minister Bernard Pons who told reporters: "I promised nothing, I gave nothing and I demanded nothing."
Talks with the unions, who had said they were trying to force the government to put pressure on employers to make concessions, could start on Thursday.
Pons said the conflict was a private one between employers and employees but he had appealed to all involved "to keep the interest of the general public in mind."
The truck drivers have blockaded fuel depots and cut supplies to supermarkets to press their demands for big wage rises, shorter working hours and the right for drivers to retire at 55 instead of 60.

Thousands of trucks continued to barricade roads and motorways in dozens of locations around the country and thousands more stood idle on parking lots, raising fears of repeat of a 1992 truckers' blockade that paralysed France.
"The truckers are really angry. They are tired, they have no money and no family life. They are exhausted at 40," a spokesman for the Communist-led CGT trade union said.
The strike has spread to Paris, which had been spared so far, and lorries have started blocking traffic on the motorway around the capital.
Drivers have begun preventing tankers leaving oil refineries to cut supplies to petrol stations and reports said petrol was already difficult to obtain in some areas of Normandy.
Depots were blocked in Bordeaux and Caen. The major Royal Dutch/Shell refinery of Berre near Marseille was also cut off but a spokesman said refinery operations continued normally.

Truckers have singled out Bordeaux, whose mayor is Prime Minister Alain Juppe, as the main focus of protests, causing huge traffic jams on all access roads. Airlines at Bordeaux airport said air freight was badly hit.

There were roadblocks in the south near Toulouse, on the A9 motorway to Spain between Nimes and Montpellier and near Avignon, in the west around Caen, Le Mans and Rennes and on the motorway between Paris and Rouen. Lyon in the centre and Lille in the north were also hit.
In the east, truckers lifted a three-day blockade of Strasbourg's Europe Bridge between France and Germany and went on to cut off the motorway to Paris.
